'''Hakkâri Province''' ({{IPA|tr|hacːaːɾi|pron}}, {{langx|tr|Hakkâri ili}}; {{langx|ku-Latn|Parêzgeha Colemêrg}}<ref>{{cite news |title=Li Colemêrgê boriyên gaza xwezayî hatin danîn |url=https://www.rudaw.net/kurmanci/kurdistan/2307201916 |access-date=27 April 2020 |agency=Rûdaw |date=23 July 2019 |language=ku}}</ref>), is a [[Provinces of Turkey|province]] in the southeast of [[Turkey]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Türkiye Mülki İdare Bölümleri Envanteri |url=https://www.e-icisleri.gov.tr/Anasayfa/MulkiIdariBolumleri.aspx |access-date=19 December 2022 |website=T.C. İçişleri Bakanlığı |language=tr |archive-date=6 July 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150706215822/https://www.e-icisleri.gov.tr/Anasayfa/MulkiIdariBolumleri.aspx |url-status=dead }}</ref> It borders [[Van Province]] to the north, and [[Şırnak Province]] to the west. The administrative centre is the city of [[Hakkâri (city)|Hakkâri]]. Its area is 7,095&nbsp;km<sup>2</sup>,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.harita.gov.tr/uploads/files-folder/il_ilce_alanlari.xlsx|title=İl ve İlçe Yüz ölçümleri|publisher=General Directorate of Mapping|access-date=19 September 2023}}</ref> and its population is 287,625 (2023).<ref name=tuik/> The current Governor is Ali Çelik.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.hakkari.gov.tr/yoneticilerimiz|title=Yöneticilerimiz|publisher=Hakkari Valiliği|access-date=22 October 2023}}</ref> The province encompasses 8 [[Belde|municipalities]], 140 villages and 313 hamlets.<ref name=":3" /> The province is considered part of [[Turkish Kurdistan]] and has a [[Kurds|Kurdish]] majority.<ref>{{cite book|last=Watts|first=Nicole F.|title=Activists in Office: Kurdish Politics and Protest in Turkey (Studies in Modernity and National Identity)|date=2010|publisher=University of Washington Press|location=Seattle|isbn=978-0-295-99050-7|page=167|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yXWl40KJfKEC&pg=PA167 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Izreʿel|first1=Shlomo|title=Language and Culture in the Near East|last2=Drory|first2=Rina|publisher=BRILL|year=1995|isbn=9789004104570|location=|pages=244}}</ref>
[[File:Sat glacier lakes.jpg|thumb|Sat glacier lakes]]
[[File:Zap Nehri.jpg|thumb|The river [[Great Zab]] in Hakkâri Province]]
[[File:Cennet Cehennem Vadisi - Hakkari Dağları.jpg|235px|thumb|Heaven and Hell Valley, Hakkari Mountains]]
[[File:Hakkâri Cilo Dağları.jpg|thumb|Hakkâri Cilo Mountains]]
The province is a stronghold for [[Kurdish nationalism]] and a hotspot in the [[Kurdish–Turkish conflict (1978–present)|Kurdish–Turkish conflict]].<ref>{{Cite news|last=Birch|first=Nicholas|date=21 May 2010|title=PKK's Nihilism Fostering Divisions among Turkey's Kurds|work=Eurasia|url=https://eurasianet.org/pkks-nihilism-fostering-divisions-among-turkeys-kurds}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Kissane|first=Bill|title=After Civil War: Division, Reconstruction, and Reconciliation in Contemporary Europe|publisher=[[University of Pennsylvania Press]]|year=2014|isbn=9780812290301|pages=170}}</ref>

== Districts ==
[[File:Hakkari districts.png|thumb|right|300px|Districts of Hakkâri province]]
Hakkâri province is divided into five [[Districts of Turkey|districts]] (capital district in '''bold'''):
*[[Çukurca District]]
*[[Derecik District]] (since 2018)
*[[Hakkâri District]]
*[[Şemdinli District]]
*[[Yüksekova District]]

== Demographics ==
Hakkari Province is located in [[Turkish Kurdistan]]<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Kreyenbroek|first1=Philip G.|title=Kurdish Culture and Identity|last2=Allison|first2=Christine|publisher=Zed Books|year=1966|isbn=9781856493291|pages=143}}</ref> and has an overwhelmingly [[Kurds|Kurdish]] population.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Watts|first1=Nicole F.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yXWl40KJfKEC&q=Kars+%28about+20+percent+Kurdish%29&pg=PA167|title=Activists in Office: Kurdish Politics and Protest in Turkey (Studies in Modernity and National Identity)|date=2010|publisher=University of Washington Press|isbn=9780295990507|language=en}}</ref> The province is [[Kurdish tribes|tribal]] and most of the [[Kurds]] adhere to the [[Shafiʽi school]] of [[Sunni Islam]] with the [[Naqshbandi]] order having a strong presence around [[Şemdinli]].<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2007|title=124 - Proche-Orient, géopolitique de la crise (premier trimestre 2007) Le Kurdistan irakien|journal=Hérodote|language=fr}}</ref> The Kurdish tribes in the province include the [[Doski]], Ertuşi, Gerdi, [[Herki (tribe)|Herki]], Jirki and Pinyaniş.<ref>{{cite book |title=aşiretler Raporu |date=2014 |publisher=Kaynak Yayınları |isbn=978-975-343-220-7 |pages=153–159 |edition=3 |language=tr}}</ref> The area had a significant [[Christianity|Christian]] [[Assyrian people|Assyrian]] population from various tribes before the [[Assyrian genocide]] in 1915. The Assyrian tribes in the region were [[Jilu (tribe)|Jilu]], Dez, [[Baz (tribe)|Baz]], [[Tkhuma (tribe)|Tkhuma]], Tal and [[Tyari (tribe)|Tyari]].<ref name="Becker">{{cite book|last1=Becker|first1=Adam H.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DbTtBgAAQBAJ&q=hakkari+tribes&pg=PA47|title=Revival and Awakening: American Evangelical Missionaries in Iran and the Origins of Assyrian Nationalism|date=2015|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=9780226145457|page=47|language=en}}</ref> Relations between [[Assyrians]] and [[Kurds]] have been described as a 'tense coexistence' due to the ability to coexist despite the recurring disputes over land and life stock, and robbery of each other and of travelers. Assyrian resentment in the region was more directed towards the Ottomans than the Kurds, due to the Ottoman hostility towards the Christian minority, viewing them as a disloyal non-Muslim component.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|title=Hakkari|url=https://gedsh.bethmardutho.org/entry/Hakkari?fq=;fq-Browse:Browse;H;|access-date=21 November 2020|website=Gorgias Encyclopedic Dictionary of the Syriac Heritage: Electronic Edition| last1=Coakley | first1=James F. }}</ref>

Hakkari Sanjak, part of [[Van vilayet]], had a population of 5,896 in 1881-1882 of which {{Percentage|4830|5896|1}} was Muslim and {{Percentage|1066|5896|1}} Christian.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Karpat|first=Kemal|title=Ottoman population 1830-1914|publisher=[[The University of Wisconsin Press]]|year=1985|isbn=9780299091606|location=|pages=146}}</ref>

In the 1945 census, {{Percentage|34688|35124|1}} of the population was Muslim, while [[Jews]] constituted the largest religious minority with {{Percentage|34|35124|1}}. Only one Christian was enumerated in 1945, from the [[Protestantism|Protestant]] denomination.{{sfnp|Dündar|2000|p=176}} In the same census, [[Kurdish languages|Kurdish]] and [[Turkish language|Turkish]] were the first language for {{Percentage|30830|35124|1}} and {{Percentage|4002|35124|1}} of the population.{{sfnp|Dündar|2000|p=177}} The Jewish population left for [[Israel]] shortly after 1948.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Özgen|first=Özden|date=2016|title=Hakkari bölgesinde yaşamış dini topluluklar|url=https://dergipark.org.tr/tr/download/article-file/353720|journal=İnsan Kaynakları ve Eğitim Müdürü|language=tr|page=48}}</ref> In the 1950 census, {{Percentage|39552|44207|1}} of the population spoke [[Kurdish languages|Kurdish]] as first language, while the second largest first language was Turkish at {{Percentage|3977|44207|1}}.{{sfnp|Dündar|2000|p=186}} In the subsequent census of 1955, Kurdish constituted the first language for {{Percentage|48446|54824|1}} of the population and Turkish for {{Percentage|6295|54824|1}}. The same census found {{Percentage|54809|54824|1}} of the population to be Muslim.{{sfnp|Dündar|2000|pp=197-198}} Kurdish and Turkish remained the two largest first languages in the 1960 census for {{Percentage|54655|67766|1}} and {{Percentage|13033|67766|1}} of the population, respectively.{{sfnp|Dündar|2000|p=207}} As with the previous census, Muslims constituted {{Percentage|67740|67766|1}} of the population.{{sfnp|Dündar|2000|p=211}} In the last census conducted in Turkey in 1965, Kurdish remained the largest first language with {{Percentage|72365|83937|1}}, while Turkish remained the second largest first language at {{Percentage|10357|83937|1}}.{{sfnp|Dündar|2000|p=218}} {{Percentage|83221|83937|1}} of the population was Muslim and {{Percentage|704|83937|1}} was Christian in 1965.{{sfnp|Dündar|2000|p=222}}

In 1980, the only language spoken in rural parts was Kurdish while both Kurdish and Turkish were spoken in urban areas, due to the presence of military and civil officials from other parts of Turkey.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book|title=Ethnic Groups in the Republic of Turkey|year=1989|editor-last=Peter Alfred|editor-first=Andrews|pages=212|editor-last2=Benninghaus|editor-first2=Rüdiger}}</ref>

==History==
In the 14th century, [[Timur]] devastated the urban centers of Mesopotamia. His conquest of Baghdad and especially the destruction of [[Tikrit]] affected the Syrian Orthodox Church, which sheltered near Nineveh at [[Mar Mattai Monastery]]. Following the destruction of Christians in the region, the Ismailis and Sunni and Shi'a Muslims were attacked indiscriminately by [[Timur]] during the second part of the 14th century. The few survivors sought refuge among the Assyrians of Hakkari and the surrounding region. This region also produced many bishops and patriarchs as hereditary succession was used to prevent a full ecclesiastical collapse of the church. By the 16th century, the Assyrians disappeared from many cities where they previously thrived, such as in [[Tabriz]] and [[Nisibis]]. The head of the [[Church of the East]] moved from [[Baghdad]] to [[Maragheh]] by 1553.<ref name="Alexander36">{{Harvnb|Alexander|1994|p=36}}</ref>

=== Ottoman control ===
{{Main|Emirate of Hakkâri}}
[[File:A portrait of a Kurdish fighter from the Hakkari region, Alexander Orłowski, St Petersburg, Russia, circa 1819 or after.jpg|thumb|Portrait of a Kurdish fighter from the Hakkâri region (1819)]]
Although the region was nominally under [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] control since the 16th century, it was administered as [[Emirate of Hakkâri]] by its Kurdish inhabitants.{{sfn|Aboona|2008|p=2}}<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sinclair |first=T. A. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EK1EBAAAQBAJ |title=Eastern Turkey: An Architectural & Archaeological Survey, Volume I |date=1989-12-31 |publisher=Pindar Press |isbn=978-0-907132-32-5 |pages=340 |language=en}}</ref> Kurds also settled [[Armenians|Armenian]] farmers in the region.<ref name=":03">{{Cite book|last=Eppel|first=Michael|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-tuPDAAAQBAJ|title=A People Without a State: The Kurds from the Rise of Islam to the Dawn of Nationalism|date=2016|publisher=University of Texas Press|isbn=9781477311073|pages=58}}</ref> The situation changed after the Badr Khan rule and the [[Tanzimat]] reforms as the Ottomans were now able to extend their full control unopposed.<ref name="Aboona3">{{Harvnb|Aboona|2008|p=3}}</ref> The region was part of [[Van Vilayet]] during the Ottoman era as ''Hakkari sanjak'' with [[Başkale]] serving as capital, except from 1880 to 1888 where it was elevated to [[vilayet]] status.<ref name=":2" /> As of 1920, Hakkari was producing [[lead]]. The lead, which came from a government owned mine, was used to make [[bullet]]s.<ref name="Prothero71">{{cite book|last=Prothero|first=W. G.|url=http://www.wdl.org/en/item/11768/view/1/71/|title=Armenia and Kurdistan|publisher=H.M. Stationery Office|year=1920|location=London|page=71}}</ref>

==== Massacres of Badr Khan ====
{{main|Massacres of Badr Khan}}
In the 19th century, several competing Kurdish centers began emerging in the region. Mir Muhammed, the Kurdish Emir of the [[Soran Emirate]], situated around [[Rawandiz]] was able to depose his rivals and control a region stretching from [[Mardin]] to [[Persian Azerbaijan]].<ref name="Aboona173">{{Harvnb|Aboona|2008|p=173}}</ref>
The Ottomans, seeking to consolidate their control of the region, engaged him in a costly war which eventually led to the dissolution of his Emirate.<ref name="Aboona174">{{Harvnb|Aboona|2008|p=174}}</ref> After the fall of his main rival, [[Bedir Khan Beg]] of [[Bohtan]] sought to extend his dominion by annexing the Assyrian regions in Hakkari.<ref name="Aboona179">{{Harvnb|Aboona|2008|p=179}}</ref> He took advantage of a rift between the patriarch [[Shimun XVII Abraham]] and Nur Allah, the Emir of Hakkari. Bedir Khan allied with Nur Allah and attacked the Assyrians of Hakkari in the summer of 1843, massacring them and taking those who survived as slaves. Another massacre was inflicted in 1846 on the Tyari tribe, also residing in Hakkari. The western powers, alarmed by the massacres pressured the Ottomans to intervene and the Emir of Bohtan was ultimately defeated and exiled to [[Crete]] in 1847.<ref name="McDowall47">{{Harvnb|McDowall|2000|p=47}}</ref>

==== Genocide and exodus ====
On the eve of the First World War, patriarch [[Shimun XIX Benyamin]] was promised preferential treatment in anticipation of the war.<ref name="Stafford23">{{Harvnb|Stafford|2006|p=23}}</ref> Shortly after the war began, however, Assyrian and Armenian settlements to the north of Hakkari were attacked and sacked by Kurdish irregulars allied with the Ottoman Army in the [[Assyrian genocide]].<ref name="Stafford24">{{Harvnb|Stafford|2006|p=24}}</ref><ref name="gaunt134">{{Harvnb|Gaunt|Beṯ-Şawoce|2006|p=134}}</ref> Others were forced into [[Ottoman labour battalions|labour battalions]] and later executed.<ref name="gaunt136">{{Harvnb|Gaunt|Beṯ-Şawoce|2006|p=136}}</ref>

The turning point was when the patriarch's brother was taken prisoner as he was studying in [[Constantinople]]. The Ottomans demanded Assyrian neutrality and executed him as a warning.<ref name="stafford25">{{Harvnb|Stafford|2006|p=25}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Yusuf|first=Malik|title=The Assyrian Tragedy|url=http://www.aina.org/books/tat.htm|access-date=2020-05-20|website=www.aina.org}}</ref> In return, the patriarch declared war on the Ottomans on 10 April 1915.<ref name="stafford25" />

The Assyrians were immediately attacked by Kurdish irregulars backed by the Ottomans, driving most of the Assyrians of Hakkari to the mountain tops, as those who stayed in their villages were killed.<ref name="stafford25" /> Shimun Benjamin was able to move unnoticed to [[Urmia]], which at the time was under [[Imperial Russia|Russian]] control, and tried to persuade them to send a relief force to the besieged Assyrians.<ref name="stafford25" /> When the Russians replied that the request was unreasonable, he returned to Hakkari and led the surviving 50,000 Assyrians through the mountains to safety in Urmia.<ref name="stafford25" /> Thousands perished from cold and hunger during this march.<ref name="stafford25" /> In 1924, Turkey expelled the last Christian inhabitants in the region.<ref name="Nisan188">{{Harvnb|Nisan|2002|p=188}}</ref>

=== In Turkey ===
In order to [[Turkification|Turkify]] the local population,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/867135/65687_13.pdf|title=Young Turk social engineering : mass violence and the nation state in eastern Turkey, 1913- 1950|last=Üngör|first=Umut|website=University of Amsterdam|pages=244–247|access-date=8 April 2020}}</ref> in June 1927 the Law 1164 was passed<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://dergipark.org.tr/en/download/article-file/20607|title=Üçüncü Umumi Müfettişliği'nin Kurulması ve III. Umumî Müfettiş Tahsin Uzer'in Bazı Önemli Faaliyetleri|last=Aydogan|first=Erdal|access-date=8 April 2020}}</ref> which allowed the creation of Inspectorates-General (''Umumi Müffetişlik,'' UM).<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last=Bayir|first=Derya|title=Minorities and Nationalism in Turkish Law|date=2016-04-22|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-317-09579-8|pages=139|language=en}}</ref> The province therefore was included in the so-called [[First Inspectorate-General (Turkey)|First Inspectorate General]], which span over the provinces of Hakkâri, [[Siirt Province|Siirt]], Van, [[Mardin Province|Mardin]], [[Bitlis Province|Bitlis]], [[Şanlıurfa Province|Sanlıurfa]], [[Elazığ Province|Elaziğ]], and [[Diyarbakır Province|Diyarbakır]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Jongerden|first=Joost|title=The Settlement Issue in Turkey and the Kurds: An Analysis of Spatical Policies, Modernity and War|date=2007-01-01|publisher=BRILL|isbn=978-90-04-15557-2|pages=53|language=en}}</ref> The first UM was created on the 1 January 1928 and centered in Diyarbakır.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/867135/65687_13.pdf|title=Young Turk social engineering : mass violence and the nation state in eastern Turkey, 1913- 1950|last=Umut|first=Üngör|website=University of Amsterdam|page=258|access-date=8 April 2020}}</ref> The UM was governed by an [[Inspectorates-General (Turkey)|Inspector General]], who governed with a wide-ranging authority over civilian, juridical and military matters.<ref name=":1" /> The office of the Inspector General was dissolved in 1952 during the government of the [[Democrat Party (Turkey, 1946–61)|Democrat Party]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Bozarslan|first=Hamit|title=The Cambridge History of Turkey|date=2008-04-17|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-62096-3|editor-last=Fleet|editor-first=Kate|pages=343|language=en|editor-last2=Faroqhi|editor-first2=Suraiya|editor-last3=Kasaba|editor-first3=Reşat|editor-last4=Kunt|editor-first4=I. Metin}}</ref> Hakkari though was still banned for foreign citizens until 1965.<ref name=":0" />

From July 1987 to August 2002 Hakkari was within the [[OHAL]] state of emergency region.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.refworld.org/pdfid/414d86ab4.pdf|title=Case of Dogan and others v. Turkey|page=21|access-date=12 November 2019}}</ref> It was Governed by a so-called Supergovernor, who was invested with additional powers than a normal Governor. He was given authority over all the other provincial Governors in the OHAL area and also the power to permanently relocate and resettle the village's population.<ref name=":02">{{Cite book|last=Jongerden|first=Joost|title=The Settlement Issue in Turkey and the Kurds|publisher=Brill|year=2007|isbn=978-90-47-42011-8|pages=141–142}}</ref>
